opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, open-endedness is really the missing ingredient if we want to get to artificial superhuman intelligence. What we've seen with foundation models is incredible progress, but fundamentally they're trained on human-generated data, which means they're, in a sense, bounded by what humans have already written down. If you want systems that go beyond that, that discover genuinely new knowledge, you need some process that can keep generating novel and learnable artifacts on its own.

In our position paper, we tried to pin down what we actually mean by open-endedness, because it's often used quite vaguely. The definition we landed on is from the perspective of an observer: a system is open-ended if it keeps producing artifacts that are both novel and learnable to that observer. Novelty means the artifacts become increasingly unpredictable given the observer's current model; learnability means that, given the history of artifacts, the observer can actually get better at predicting them. So it's not just random noise, which would be novel but not learnable, and it's not something that converges, which would be learnable but eventually stops being novel. It's this sweet spot where you keep being surprised, but in a way you can make sense of.

And I think the really exciting thing now is that foundation models give us a fantastic substrate to build on. Historically, open-endedness research, things like evolutionary algorithms, POET-style environment generation, or quality-diversity methods, struggled because they lacked a good notion of what humans would find interesting. Foundation models encode a lot of that prior. So you can use them as mutation operators, as models of interestingness, as generators of new tasks and environments, and then couple that with reinforcement learning, self-improvement, and automated evaluation, so the system keeps pushing its own frontier.

Concretely, I see a few directions. One is reinforcement learning with self-generated curricula, where agents propose their own tasks at the edge of their capability. Another is self-improvement loops, where models generate data, critique it, and retrain on what's useful. Then there's work on automating parts of the scientific process itself, models proposing hypotheses, running experiments, writing code, and evaluating results. And we've done work like Rainbow Teaming, where you use open-ended search to find diverse adversarial prompts, which shows these ideas already have practical value today, including for safety.

Which brings me to the last point: safety and responsibility matter enormously here. An open-ended system is by definition one that produces things you can't fully predict. That's the point, but it's also the risk. So we need to think carefully about keeping humans in the loop, making artifacts interpretable and learnable to us as observers, not just to the system itself. In a way, the observer-relative definition helps: if we insist that what the system produces stays learnable to humans, we get both the benefits of discovery and some handle on understanding where it's going.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can generate novel artifacts and push their frontier, but does not identify discovered artifacts as stepping stones enabling future progress.

r002.rationale: It says systems keep producing novel and learnable artifacts, but does not state that they accumulate more interesting artifacts as they run longer.

r003.rationale: The response presents foundation models as a useful substrate, but does not predict that most near-term open-ended-systems work will focus on LLM-based systems.

r004.rationale: It mentions automated evaluation and self-improvement loops, but does not describe collected empirical evidence as feedback that helps LLM-based exploratory systems improve themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it, the core idea is that if you want a system that eventually exceeds human capabilities, you can't get there by purely imitating human-generated data. At some point you run out of that data, and more fundamentally, a model trained to imitate us is anchored to us. So the question becomes: where does novel knowledge come from? And my answer is that it has to come from open-ended processes, systems that generate their own curriculum of problems, solve them, and in doing so keep producing artifacts that are both novel and learnable from the perspective of the observer.

That framing, novel and learnable, is really the heart of it. Something like AlphaGo's move 37 was novel, it surprised the experts, but it was also learnable, in the sense that humans could study it afterwards and understand why it worked. Pure randomness is novel but not learnable. Something you've already seen is learnable but not novel. Open-endedness lives in that sweet spot, and it's observer-dependent, which I think is important because it tells you a superhuman system has to be open-ended relative to us.

Concretely, I think you need a few ingredients. You need foundation models, because they carry this enormous prior about what humans find interesting, which is a huge help in steering search. You need environments or problem generators that can keep scaling in complexity, whether that's self-play, co-evolution of agents and tasks, or models proposing their own research problems and verifying the solutions. And you need some form of search over that space, whether that's evolutionary methods, tree search, or just sampling with good filters. Put those together and you get a loop where the system is the author of its own training distribution, not just a consumer of ours.

Where I think this gets genuinely exciting, and also a bit humbling, is that the same loop can turn inward. You can have systems that propose improvements to their own learning algorithms, their own scaffolding, their own prompts, and keep what works. That's the direction I expect the field to go, and it raises a lot of safety questions we should be taking seriously now, because once a system is generating its own goals and knowledge, oversight becomes a real engineering problem rather than a philosophical one.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is to build systems that don’t just solve the tasks we give them, but continually discover new problems worth solving. Most of our training setups today have a fairly fixed objective and a fixed distribution of data. You can become extremely capable within that setup, but there’s a question of where the next challenge comes from.

In an open-ended system, generating challenges and learning to solve them would happen together. Imagine an agent exploring an environment, developing a new skill, and thereby unlocking situations it couldn’t encounter before. Those situations demand further skills. You get a feedback loop in which the space of possibilities keeps expanding.

The difficult part is that novelty alone isn’t enough. A system can produce endless variation without producing anything interesting or useful. We need mechanisms that encourage challenges that are learnable, that build on previous discoveries, and that lead to increasingly general capabilities. And we need ways to preserve those discoveries rather than continually forgetting them.

My intuition is that this could be an important ingredient for superhuman intelligence, because we wouldn’t have to anticipate every task or manually specify every step of a curriculum. But it’s not a guarantee. We still have to understand how to steer that process so that growing capability translates into things we actually value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to build systems that keep generating their own challenges, rather than solving a fixed task and then stopping. You have this interplay between discovering something new, learning how to deal with it, and opening up further possibilities. The environment changes as the agent becomes more capable, so there’s always another frontier.

The hard part is making that process productive. Novelty alone isn’t enough. A system can generate endless variation without discovering anything useful. We need mechanisms that encourage exploration while allowing skills and knowledge to accumulate—and sometimes that means preserving stepping stones whose value isn’t obvious at the time.

So I envision something closer to an evolving ecosystem than a single model optimizing one objective. Agents propose challenges, other agents learn to solve them, and their interactions create new challenges. Whether that can lead to broadly superhuman intelligence is still an open question. But I think learning how to sustain that cycle of discovery is a very promising direction.
